ATHENS, Greece (CNN) -- Authorities vowed to re-impose order after demonstrators rose up across Greece Monday in a third day of rioting over Saturday's killing of a 15-year-old boy that has left dozens injured and scores of properties destroyed. An undated photo of Alexandros Grigoropoulos, whose death has sparked riots across Greece. "Under no circumstances will the government accept what is occurring," said Greek Interior Minister Prokopis Pavlopoulos. "We will do what is necessary." It was unclear what would be necessary to placate the demonstrators. "We've just lost count of how many demonstrations are taking place now," a police spokesman in Athens told CNN. Police said 34 civilians and 16 police officers were injured Monday in rioting that spread into new municipalities, including Trikala, Larissam and Veria. Riots broke out Saturday in Thessaloniki and Athens, where police killed the teen.  Watch the latest report on the rioting » . Demonstrators had torched three government buildings and three offices of the ruling conservative political party in downtown Athens, a National Fire Brigade spokesman told Greek state television. Watch as iReporter witnesses the clashes . Thirty-five cars and 160 trash containers also had been set ablaze, he said.  See images of anarchy on Greek streets » . Demonstrators Monday barricaded streets in Athens and Thessaloniki and hurled gasoline bombs as they battled with police. Clouds of tear gas hung over the capital city as riot police continued to battle the hundreds of young self-styled anarchists rioting over the boy's death. "Rage is what I feel for what has happened, rage, and that this cop who did it must see what it is to kill a kid and to destroy a life," a student in Athens told reporters Monday.  Watch protesters clash with police » . In a nationally televised address broadcast on state television, Greek Prime Minister Kostas Karamanlis condemned the violence and promised to punish those responsible for Saturday's shooting. He also announced a decision to drop plans to reimburse business owners affected by the rioting. The police officer who fired the fatal shot has been charged with "manslaughter with intent" and suspended from duty, police said, adding that a second police officer was arrested Saturday on criminal accessory charges. Government officials have condemned the shooting. "An investigation is under way and those found responsible will be punished," said Pavlopoulos. "Measures will also be taken to avoid such incidents again in the future." iReport.com: Are you there? Share photos, video of rioting . On Monday, authorities conducted an autopsy on the teenage boy in an effort to answer questions about the circumstances of the shooting, but the boy's family has called in their own investigators to verify state findings, the Athens coroner told CNN. The U.S. and British embassies issued warnings to employees and tourists on Sunday, instructing them to avoid downtown Athens and other major cities until rioting subsides. Tourists in central Athens hotels were advised by hotel staff not to leave their rooms as police fanned out across the city. "There are lots of burning bins and debris in the street and a huge amount of tear gas in the air, which we got choked with on the way back to our hotel," according to Joel Brown, a CNN senior press officer visiting Athens on Sunday. A police statement about the teenage boy's death said the incident started when six young protesters pelted a police patrol car with stones. The teen was shot as he tried to throw a petrol bomb at the officers, police said. Other angry teens converged on the site almost immediately. Fighting between youths and police erupted elsewhere, including Thessaloniki, the country's second-largest city. Hundreds of young people took to the streets of the sprawling port city, finally barricading themselves behind the gates of a state university. Authorities have been barred from entering university grounds since tanks crushed a 1973 student uprising protesting the ruling military junta. It was not clear what authorities would do about the demonstrators still holed up at the university. No deaths have been reported since Saturday. Police said Monday that 20 protesters had been rounded up for questioning. Journalist Anthee Carassava in Athens contributed to this report.

# Greece Erupts in Violence Following Teen's Death

Greek officials pledged Monday to restore control as the country entered its third consecutive day of unrest, sparked by the fatal shooting of a 15-year-old boy on Saturday. The chaos has resulted in numerous injuries and widespread property damage.

Interior Minister Prokopis Pavlopoulos issued a firm statement: "The government will not tolerate these events under any circumstances. We will take whatever action is required." However, the specific measures needed to calm protesters remained undefined.

An Athens police representative admitted to CNN that officials had "lost track of exactly how many separate demonstrations are happening." According to police reports, Monday's clashes left 34 civilians and 16 officers wounded, with unrest spreading to additional towns including Trikala, Larissa, and Veria. The initial violence had erupted Saturday in both Thessaloniki and Athens—the city where police shot the teenager.

Government buildings bore the brunt of protester rage in central Athens. A National Fire Brigade representative told Greek state television that rioters set fire to three government offices along with three branches belonging to the ruling conservative party. Additionally, 35 vehicles and 160 garbage containers were burned.

On Monday, protesters constructed barricades throughout Athens and Thessaloniki, launching Molotov cocktails at police forces. Tear gas blanketed the capital as officers confronted hundreds of self-identified anarchist youths demanding accountability for the boy's death. One Athens student expressed the prevailing sentiment to reporters: "What I feel is rage—rage that this officer took a life, and he needs to understand what it means to kill a child and destroy that future."

Prime Minister Kostas Karamanlis addressed the nation via state television, denouncing the violence while vowing that those responsible for Saturday's shooting would face justice. He also reversed an earlier decision, announcing that business owners suffering losses from the riots would not receive government compensation.

Regarding the shooting itself, the officer who fired the fatal shot now faces charges of "manslaughter with intent" and has been suspended pending investigation. Police confirmed a second officer was arrested Saturday for criminal complicity. Pavlopoulos emphasized: "An investigation is underway, and responsible parties will face consequences. We will also implement measures to prevent similar tragedies going forward."

An autopsy was performed Monday to clarify the circumstances surrounding the boy's death, though his family has enlisted independent investigators to cross-check official findings, according to the Athens coroner who spoke with CNN.

Both the American and British embassies issued advisories Sunday urging staff and visiting tourists to steer clear of downtown Athens and other urban centers until the disturbances calm. Hotel personnel in central Athens recommended guests remain indoors as police patrols expanded citywide. CNN senior press officer Joel Brown, present in Athens Sunday, described the scene: "The streets were filled with burning trash and debris, and tear gas was so thick in the air that we ended up choking on it walking back to our hotel."

According to official police accounts, the shooting incident began when six young demonstrators threw rocks at a police patrol vehicle. Officers claim the teenager was shot while attempting to throw a firebomb at them. Within moments, other enraged youths flooded the scene. Similar confrontations broke out in Thessaloniki, Greece's second-largest city, where hundreds of young protesters eventually retreated behind the gates of a state university—a location police have been forbidden from entering since a 1973 military crackdown crushed student demonstrations against the ruling junta at that same site. How authorities plan to handle protesters currently sheltering there remains uncertain.

While no fatalities have occurred since the initial shooting Saturday, police reported detaining 20 protesters for questioning as of Monday.

*Reporting contributed by journalist Anthee Carassava in Athens.*

# Greek Authorities Vow to Restore Order Amid Escalating National Unrest

Greek authorities have pledged to restore order across the country following three consecutive days of violent, nationwide rioting that erupted after a police officer fatally shot a 15-year-old boy on Saturday. The tragic incident has ignited widespread public outrage, plunging Greece into one of its most serious periods of civil unrest in recent years.

## Spreading Unrest Across the Nation

What began as isolated outbreaks of violence in the major cities of Thessaloniki and Athens has since spread rapidly to additional urban centers, including Trikala, Larissa, and Veria. The rapid escalation underscores the depth of public anger over the shooting and reflects broader frustrations that appear to extend beyond the immediate tragedy. On Monday alone, the violence left 34 civilians and 16 police officers injured, highlighting the intensity of the clashes and the challenges law enforcement faces in containing the unrest.

## Destruction and Confrontation in the Streets

The rioting has taken a heavy toll on public and private property. Demonstrators have set fire to government buildings, offices belonging to the ruling political party, numerous vehicles, and trash containers scattered throughout affected cities. Violent confrontations between protesters and police have become a defining feature of the unrest, with rioters hurling gasoline bombs at security forces, who have responded with tear gas in an effort to disperse the crowds. These volatile street battles have transformed parts of Greece's urban centers into scenes of chaos and destruction.

## Government Response and Accountability

In a televised address to the nation, Prime Minister Kostas Karamanlis publicly condemned the violence sweeping across Greece, calling for an end to the destruction while acknowledging the gravity of the situation. Karamanlis pledged that his government would ensure accountability for those responsible for the boy's death, seeking to reassure a deeply angered public that justice would be pursued through proper channels. His address represented an attempt to balance the need for law and order with recognition of the legitimate grievances driving the protests.

## Public Demands for Justice

At the heart of the unrest lies a profound sense of anger and grief among demonstrators, who have taken to the streets to demand accountability and justice for the young victim. Protesters have been vocal in their insistence that the police officer responsible for the shooting fully comprehend the severity of his actions and face appropriate consequences for taking the life of a child. This demand for justice has become a rallying cry uniting demonstrators across the affected cities, transforming individual grief into a collective call for systemic accountability within Greece's law enforcement institutions.

As the situation continues to unfold, the coming days will likely prove critical in determining whether the government's pledges of accountability can help quell the unrest, or whether the underlying tensions will continue to fuel further confrontation between citizens and authorities.

Athens, Greece — For the third consecutive day, Greece has been rocked by widespread rioting that shows no signs of abating, as public anger over the fatal police shooting of a 15-year-old boy continues to boil over into the streets of major cities across the nation.

The unrest, which began Saturday night after the teenager was killed during an confrontation with police in the Exarchia district of Athens, has since metastasized into one of the most serious outbreaks of civil disorder Greece has witnessed in years. What started as spontaneous protests has evolved into organized and increasingly violent demonstrations, with crowds of youths and activists taking to the streets in open defiance of authorities.

Athens has borne the brunt of the chaos, with rioters setting fire to government buildings, smashing storefronts, and torching dozens of vehicles in running battles with riot police. Thick clouds of smoke have hung over parts of the capital as protesters hurled petrol bombs and paving stones, while police responded with tear gas and stun grenades in an effort to disperse the crowds.

The unrest has not been confined to the capital alone. Thessaloniki, Greece's second-largest city, has seen similarly intense clashes, with protesters clashing with police near government offices and commercial districts. Reports of violence have also emerged from Trikala and other cities, suggesting that the anger over the shooting has struck a broader nerve across Greek society, tapping into existing frustrations over police conduct, economic hardship, and government accountability.

Officials report that the violence has left dozens of people injured, including both protesters and police officers, while the property damage across affected cities has been extensive. Businesses have shuttered, public transportation has been disrupted, and entire neighborhoods have taken on the appearance of war zones in the aftermath of the clashes.

The Greek government has moved to address the crisis, with the Interior Minister issuing public statements condemning the violence while simultaneously acknowledging the legitimacy of public anger over the shooting. The minister has pledged a thorough investigation into the incident and promised that those responsible for the boy's death will face appropriate legal consequences.

Prime Minister has also weighed in, calling for calm while vowing that the government will act swiftly to restore order to the affected cities. In public remarks, he emphasized the need for accountability within law enforcement while urging protesters to express their grievances through peaceful means rather than continued violence.

Despite these assurances, the situation remains highly volatile. Riot police have been deployed in greater numbers across multiple cities, and there are growing concerns that the unrest could continue to spread or intensify in the coming days. Analysts and observers note that the protests appear to be tapping into deeper societal tensions, including long-standing grievances about police brutality, youth unemployment, and government responsiveness to public concerns.

As night falls once again on Greek cities, authorities remain on high alert, bracing for the possibility of further clashes. The coming days will likely prove critical in determining whether the government's promises of justice and reform can quell the unrest, or whether Greece is facing a prolonged period of civil disturbance reminiscent of past periods of social upheaval in the country's history.

This blend of ancient heritage and modern revitalization has made Athens a compelling story for international media coverage.

Whether covered for its historical significance, cultural offerings, or economic developments, Athens remains a city that consistently captures global attention. # Greece Erupts in Violence After Police Shooting of Teenager

**ATHENS, Greece** — Riots that began after police fatally shot a 15-year-old boy have spread across Greece, with protesters clashing with police, setting fires, and looting stores in some of the worst civil unrest the country has seen in decades.

The violence erupted Saturday night after Alexandros Grigoropoulos was shot and killed in the Exarchia district of Athens, a neighborhood known as a center of anarchist and leftist activity. Police said the shooting occurred after officers were confronted by a group of youths, though accounts of exactly what happened remain in dispute. The officer involved has been arrested and charged, but that has done little to quell the anger spilling into the streets.

"This wasn't just a shooting — it was the spark," said one protester in central Athens, declining to give his name. "People have been angry for a long time about police, about the economy, about corruption. This just brought it out."

By Sunday, riots had spread beyond Athens to Thessaloniki, Greece's second-largest city, as well as Patras, Volos, and other towns. Demonstrators, many of them students and young people, have thrown Molotov cocktails, smashed shop windows, and torched cars and garbage bins. Government buildings, banks, and businesses have been targeted, with dozens of storefronts destroyed in Athens' main shopping districts.

Riot police have responded with tear gas and stun grenades in an attempt to disperse crowds, but the clashes have continued night after night. Greek authorities say scores of people have been arrested and dozens more injured, including both protesters and police officers.

The unrest comes at a politically sensitive moment for Prime Minister Kostas Karamanlis, whose conservative government already faced criticism over the economy, corruption scandals, and a slim parliamentary majority. Opposition leaders have called for the resignation of the public order minister, and some are questioning whether the government can survive the crisis.

Labor unions and student groups have used the unrest as a rallying point, organizing marches that have drawn thousands into the streets of Athens in solidarity with the slain teenager and in protest of broader economic grievances, including high youth unemployment.

Shop owners in Athens have described scenes of chaos, with security shutters torn down and storefronts left in ruins. "I've never seen anything like this," said one shopkeeper near Syntagma Square, surveying the wreckage of his store. "This is not about politics anymore. This is just destruction."

International observers have expressed concern over the scale of the violence, with some drawing comparisons to unrest seen in French suburbs in 2005. European Union officials have called for calm and urged Greek authorities to exercise restraint while also addressing the underlying anger driving the protests.

Alexandros Grigoropoulos' death has become a symbol for many young Greeks who say they feel disconnected from a political system they view as unresponsive to their concerns. His funeral, held earlier this week, drew large crowds and was itself marked by clashes between mourners and police.

As night fell Monday, authorities braced for another wave of unrest, with riot police stationed throughout central Athens and businesses boarding up windows in anticipation of further violence. Government officials have promised a full investigation into the shooting, but for many demonstrators, calls for accountability have expanded into a broader indictment of the Greek state itself.

The question now facing Athens — and the Karamanlis government — is whether the anger sparked by one teenager's death can be contained, or whether it signals a deeper reckoning still to come.

*This is a developing story and will be updated.*

# Greek Capital Erupts in Violent Protests After Police Shoot Teenager

**ATHENS, Greece (CNN)** — Rioting continued for a third consecutive night in Athens and spread to at least four other Greek cities Thursday, following the fatal shooting of a 16-year-old boy by police in the central Exarcheia district, an incident that has reignited long-simmering tensions between Greek youth and law enforcement.

The teenager, identified by authorities as Alexandros Papadakis, was shot Tuesday evening during what police describe as a confrontation with officers responding to reports of vandalism. Witnesses dispute this account, claiming the shooting was unprovoked.

"He was just standing there with his friends," said Maria Konstantinou, 19, a university student who said she witnessed the shooting from a nearby café. "The police car pulled up, there was shouting, and then we heard gunshots. He never had a chance to run."

The Greek government has announced an independent investigation into the shooting, with Prime Minister Kostas Mitsotakis calling for "calm and patience" while promising accountability.

"I understand the anger. I share the grief," Mitsotakis said in a televised address Wednesday night. "But violence against our institutions, against businesses, against fellow citizens — this cannot be the answer to violence."

The two officers involved in the shooting have been suspended pending the outcome of the investigation, according to a statement from the Hellenic Police headquarters. The department did not respond to CNN's request for the officers' names or additional details about the encounter.

By Thursday morning, riot police had deployed tear gas and stun grenades in at least six locations across central Athens, including Syntagma Square and the historic Exarcheia neighborhood, long considered a center of anti-establishment sentiment. Local business owners reported extensive damage to storefronts, with several buildings set ablaze overnight.

"I've lost everything," said Yannis Papadopoulos, 54, who owns a small electronics shop near the university. Standing amid shattered glass and charred merchandise Thursday morning, he added: "I don't blame the young people for being angry. But this — this helps no one."

Protesters, many of them students, have gathered nightly chanting "Justice for Alexandros" and carrying signs reading "Stop Police Violence." Clashes between demonstrators and riot police have resulted in dozens of injuries and more than 130 arrests, according to Greek Health Ministry and police officials.

Dimitris Charalambous, a 22-year-old protester, said the demonstrations reflect frustration extending beyond the shooting itself.

"This isn't just about one boy, though his death is a tragedy," Charalambous told CNN. "This is about years of feeling like the police can do whatever they want to us, especially in neighborhoods like this one, and nothing happens."
